questions.text:
Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, ________

Fill the blank by choosing a word with a meaning similar to that of the words given above.
questions.solution:
"Expedite," "hasten," and "hurry" all mean to make something happen more quickly or speed up a process. The word matching this same meaning is "accelerate" (to speed up).

"Retard" is actually the opposite (to slow down), while "provide" and "disable" are unrelated in meaning to this group.

Answer: Accelerate

questions.text: A black square PQRS has been cut into two parts. One part of it is shown in Panel [latex]\text{I}.[/latex] Which one of the shapes in Panel [latex]\text{II}[/latex] is the other part?
questions.solution:
This is a spatial-reasoning question: a black square [latex]PQRS[/latex] has been cut into two pieces, one of which is shown in Panel I, and we must identify its complementary piece from Panel II.

The correct complementary piece must, when combined with the piece shown in Panel I (through rotation/translation as needed, without overlapping), exactly reconstruct the original square with no gaps and no extra area. Checking each candidate shape against this requirement, only option (iii) has precisely the matching boundary/area needed to complete the square together with the given piece.

Answer: (iii)

questions.text: A day can only be cloudy or sunny. The probability of a day being cloudy is [latex]0.5[/latex], independent of the condition on other days. What is the probability that in any given four days, there will be three cloudy days and one sunny day?
questions.solution:
Each of the [latex]4[/latex] days is independently cloudy with probability [latex]0.5[/latex] (and sunny with probability [latex]0.5[/latex]). We want exactly [latex]3[/latex] cloudy days out of [latex]4[/latex], which follows a Binomial[latex](n=4, p=0.5)[/latex] distribution:

[latex]P(X=3)=\binom{4}{3}(0.5)^3(0.5)^1=4\times(0.5)^4=\dfrac{4}{16}=\dfrac14[/latex].

Answer: 1/4

questions.text: The values of Stock [latex]\text{A}[/latex] and Stock [latex]\text{B}[/latex] on a particular day are Rs. [latex]50[/latex] and Rs. [latex]80[/latex], respectively. An investor invests Rs. [latex]100[/latex] in Stock [latex]\text{A}[/latex] and Rs. [latex]80[/latex] in Stock [latex]\text{B}[/latex]. He sells all the stocks the next day when the value of Stock [latex]\text{A}[/latex] is Rs. [latex]55[/latex] and Stock [latex]\text{B}[/latex] is Rs. [latex]70[/latex]. The profit made by the investor is Rs. ________
questions.solution:
Stock A: Rs. [latex]100[/latex] invested at Rs. [latex]50[/latex]/share buys [latex]100/50=2[/latex] shares. Sold next day at Rs. [latex]55[/latex]/share: [latex]2\times55=110[/latex]. Profit [latex]=110-100=10[/latex].

Stock B: Rs. [latex]80[/latex] invested at Rs. [latex]80[/latex]/share buys [latex]80/80=1[/latex] share. Sold next day at Rs. [latex]70[/latex]/share: [latex]1\times70=70[/latex]. Profit [latex]=70-80=-10[/latex] (a loss).

Total profit [latex]=10+(-10)=0[/latex].

Answer: 0

questions.text:
'When it is raining, peacocks dance.'

Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
questions.solution:
The statement is [latex]\text{Raining}\Rightarrow\text{Dancing}[/latex]. The only thing logically guaranteed to also be true is its contrapositive: [latex]\neg\text{Dancing}\Rightarrow\neg\text{Raining}[/latex], i.e. "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining." A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original conditional, so it must hold whenever the original does.

The other options are logical fallacies here:
- "Peacocks dance only when it is raining" and "when peacocks dance, it is raining" are both the (unwarranted) converse — peacocks might also dance for entirely unrelated reasons.
- "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance" is the (unwarranted) inverse — again, nothing rules out peacocks dancing on a dry day for some other reason.

Answer: When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
